Perseverance Rover Breaks the Record for Total Distance Driven on Another Planet
24 photos
Photo: NASA
28.10 miles, or 45.22 kilometers. That’s what the odometer of NASA’s most recent rover to travel to Mars, Perseverance, showed on October 11. That’s a tiny distance, if you consider that it took the two-wheeler five and a half years to get there, but still the new record for total distance ever driven by any machine on any alien world.
The Perseverance landed on the Red Planet in early 2021, tasked with several missions, including the search for signs of past life. To accomplish them, the rover had to constantly move from place to place and, in doing so, became the new record holder.
The distance Perseverance covered by October 11 was enough to place it in front of the Opportunity, which, from 2004 to 2018, moved 28.06 miles (45.16 km). Even more interesting, though, is the fact that the new vehicle keeps on moving, and, at the end of its life (nobody knows when that will be), it would probably have set a pretty difficult record to beat.
The achievement announced by the American space agency this week can only be fully appreciated if one looks back at what all the previous Mars rovers achieved. Only this way can one fully appreciate what a long way Martian rovers have come since the first one touched down almost three decades ago.
Photo: NASA/JPL Back in 1997, NASA’s first Mars rover, the microwave-oven-sized Sojourner, spent 83 Martian days on the job, during which time it covered just 330 feet (100 meters). Then, the Spirit and Opportunity twins, having landed on the Red Planet in 2004, spent six and 15 years on the job, and covered 4.8 miles (7.7 km) and 28.06 miles, respectively.
The fourth NASA Mars rover, Curiosity , has clocked 23.65 miles (38.07 km) since landing in 2012, but, seeing how this machine is still operational, that will probably not be the end of its journey and its story.
If you change perspective, the numbers above paint the picture of Perseverance needing five and a half years to cover the same distance achieved by Opportunity in almost 15 years. And, strangely enough, that’s not owed to an increase in speed (the Perseverance can cover 1,351 feet or 412 meters each Martian day), but to the new rover’s self-driving capabilities, bundled together in something called the AutoNav.
The operation of the Perseverance goes a bit like this: controllers here on Earth set destinations and select waypoints the rover must pass through, but leave it up to the AutoNav to plot the best and safest course to each of them.
Photo: NASA The autonomous navigation system does this by imaging the terrain as the rover moves and creating a 3D map of potential hazards that must be avoided, using no less than 600,000 measurement points. Mind you, this real-time navigation and decision-making process takes place even when the rover travels at or near its top speed. The rover is thus capable of steering less and rolling more, while also checking its position against orbital maps.
NASA revealed that about 90 percent of the total distance covered so far was driven with the help of AutoNav . An earlier version of the solution, installed on the Opportunity and Spirit rovers, was responsible for only about five percent of the distance traveled by the two.
The record-holding rover is presently moving toward an area of the Red Planet called Idubi, moving through Lac de Charmes on the western rim of Jezero Crater, which is its landing spot. According to the people running it, all systems are still fully operational.
Knowing this, NASA recently extended, for the first time, the rover’s mission life duration and cleared it to keep going at least until 2028. On a hardware level, NASA said at the end of last year, it could live until at least 2031.
Photo: NASA Although the record-breaking distance the machine reached, and the prospect of going much, much further, are reasons enough to celebrate, there is something even more exciting in traveling far on another world: it gives the rover and its handlers the opportunity to explore areas of the planet that we’re not necessarily included in the science plan at first.
For a life-hunting tool, that’s probably more precious than anything, and it has already proved its merits. In its travels, the rover moved from an ancient lakebed into a fossilized river system, then onto the crater rim. In doing so, it uncovered a potential biosignature in a place called Cheyava Falls.
The discovery is so important that NASA says this is the closest we have ever come to finding life on Mars. Work on getting a better understanding of the finding is still ongoing, after NASA made the details public as it seeks help to either confirm or refute the finding.
Meanwhile, the Perseverance is heading to Idubi in a bid to prove or disprove the existence in the planet’s past of hydrothermal systems. After that, it targets the Rainbow Falls, a 328 feet (100 meters) block of crust uplifted by the impact that created Jezero four billion years ago.
